title: Where the summary stops
context: An environmental science student summarises a study, then uses it. A good summary is short enough to leave room for the writer's own point.
question: Click the phrase where the summary of Nakamura's study ends and the writer's own point begins.
text: Microplastic pollution is usually studied in rivers that run through towns and cities, where wastewater is an obvious source and samples are easy to collect. [[s1:{{cite:nakamura2021|integral}} sampled twelve upland rivers far from any town]] [[s2:and found microplastic fibres in every one,]] [[s3:at levels that rose after heavy rain.]] [[s4:This matters for how we think about where the problem comes from.]] [[s5:If fibres can reach remote rivers in rainfall,]] [[s6:then cleaning up urban wastewater alone will not keep them out of freshwater systems.]] [[s7:Monitoring programmes that sample only lowland, urban rivers]] [[s8:may therefore be underestimating how widespread the pollution has become, and missing one of the routes by which it spreads.]]

feedback.correct: Yes. Nakamura's study is reduced to one sentence: where she sampled, what she found, and when levels rose. From 'This matters…' the writer is using that finding to make their own argument.
feedback.early: A reasonable instinct, but that phrase is still part of the summary. Everything in the sentence that names Nakamura reports her study.
feedback.late: You've given Nakamura more than she found. Her study reported fibres in upland rivers and higher levels after rain; 'This matters…' and what follows are the writer's interpretation.

followUp.question: Which phrase goes furthest beyond what the study itself found?

options.text: "If fibres can reach remote rivers in rainfall"
options.feedback: Yes. The study found that levels rose after heavy rain; the writer infers that rain carries fibres there. The 'If' signals that this is the writer's reasoning, not a finding.
That is the study's finding, reported directly.

options.text: "usually studied in rivers that run through towns and cities"
options.feedback: That's the writer's background framing. It doesn't go beyond the study so much as set it up.

notes.text: Because this summarises the study as a whole, MLA needs no page number here.

chefsNote: Keep the summary short, then make your own point.
